introduction-why-ansible.core: Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible configures what runs on it: packages, files, services and users. It is agentless (it connects over SSH or WinRM and pushes small Python modules), describes desired state in YAML playbooks, and is idempotent, so running it twice changes nothing the second time. That makes server configuration repeatable instead of a pile of hand-run shell commands.

first_principles.problem: Fifty servers configured by hand over three years each behave slightly differently.
truths: Configuration drifts when done by hand.
Idempotent operations are safe to repeat.

analogy.title: A checklist for setting up a new kitchen
analogy.story: 'Oven installed, knives in drawer 2': if it's already done, you tick it and move on.
analogy.breaks: Humans skip items; Ansible checks every one every run.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Safe to run repeatedly; converges hosts.

code.text:
ansible web -m ansible.builtin.apt -a "name=nginx state=present" --become
# first run: changed=1
# second run: ok (no change)

check.q: Why is idempotency essential for configuration management?
check.a: It makes runs safe to repeat, so you can converge any host to the desired state regardless of its starting point.

inventory-where-are-we-going.core: The inventory tells Ansible which hosts exist and how to group them (web, db, prod, eu). Static inventories are INI or YAML files; dynamic inventories query clouds (the aws_ec2 plugin) by tags at runtime, so autoscaled instances are always included. Variables can be attached to hosts or groups through group_vars and host_vars.

first_principles.problem: A hand-maintained hosts file misses new autoscaled instances, which never get patched.

analogy.title: A delivery driver's address list
analogy.story: A printed list goes stale; a live dispatch app always shows today's addresses.
analogy.breaks: Addresses rarely vanish; instances churn hourly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Groups like role_web appear automatically from tags.

code.text:
# inventory/aws_ec2.yml
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions: [us-east-1]
filters:
  tag:Env: prod
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: role
hostnames: [private-ip-address]

check.q: Why prefer dynamic inventory in the cloud?
check.a: It queries the provider at runtime, so new and terminated instances are reflected automatically.

playbooks-the-to-do-list.core: A playbook is a YAML list of plays; each play targets a host group and runs an ordered list of tasks, each calling a module with arguments. Tasks report ok, changed, failed or skipped. Use `--check --diff` for a dry run, `become` for privilege escalation, and prefer purpose-built modules (apt, template, service) over shell commands so idempotency is preserved.

first_principles.problem: A playbook built from shell tasks reports 'changed' every run and can't be dry-run safely.
truths: Modules know how to check state.

analogy.title: A recipe card
analogy.story: Steps in order, each with a clear outcome; skip a step if it's already done.
analogy.breaks: Recipes don't verify; modules check current state first.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Second run reports ok for both tasks.

code.text:
- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: role_web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt: { name: nginx, state: present, update_cache: true }
    - name: Ensure nginx running
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }

check.q: Why avoid the shell module when a dedicated module exists?
check.a: Dedicated modules check current state and are idempotent; shell commands run every time and report changed.

variables-and-precedence.core: Ansible variables come from many places: role defaults, inventory group_vars and host_vars, play vars, facts gathered from hosts, registered results, and extra vars on the command line, with about 22 precedence levels. The practical rule: put tunable defaults in role defaults, environment values in group_vars, and use -e only for one-off overrides, because extra vars always win.

first_principles.problem: A port set in group_vars is mysteriously ignored because a role's vars/main.yml overrides it.
truths: Many sources can define the same variable.

analogy.title: House rules, family rules, and a parent's direct instruction
analogy.story: General rules apply unless a more specific one overrides; a direct instruction beats everything.
analogy.breaks: Families negotiate; precedence is a strict ladder.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: prod gets 8080; -e forces 9090 for one run.

code.text:
# roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml
nginx_port: 80
# inventory/group_vars/prod.yml
nginx_port: 8080
# ad-hoc override
# ansible-playbook site.yml -e nginx_port=9090

check.q: Where should a role's overridable settings live?
check.a: In defaults/main.yml, the lowest precedence, so inventory and play vars can override them.

templating-with-jinja2-filters-and-loops.core: Ansible renders Jinja2 everywhere: in task arguments ({{ var }}) and in config files via the template module. Filters transform data (default, to_nice_yaml, join, regex_replace), and loops (loop, with dict2items) repeat tasks. Templates keep a single config file that adapts per host, and template only reports changed when the rendered output differs.

first_principles.problem: Separate nginx.conf copies per environment drift out of sync.
truths: Configs differ by a few values.

analogy.title: A form letter
analogy.story: One letter with blanks for name and address, printed per recipient.
analogy.breaks: Letters aren't syntax-checked; use validate to test configs before replacing.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Config rebuilt from inventory; validated before install.

check.q: What does the template module's validate option do?
check.a: Runs a command on the rendered file before it replaces the real one, aborting if validation fails.

handlers-doing-things-only-when-necessar.core: A handler is a task that runs only when notified by a task that reported changed, and only once at the end of the play however many tasks notified it. That's how you restart nginx only when its config actually changed, instead of on every run, which would cause needless downtime.

first_principles.problem: A playbook restarts the database on every run, causing a brief outage each time.

analogy.title: Rebooting only after installing updates
analogy.story: You don't reboot daily; only when an update says it's needed, and once after several updates.
analogy.breaks: People forget to reboot; handlers are triggered reliably.

code.text:
tasks:
  - name: Deploy nginx config
    ansible.builtin.template: { src: nginx.conf.j2, dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf }
    notify: reload nginx
handlers:
  - name: reload nginx
    ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: reloaded }

check.q: What happens to pending handlers if a later task fails?
check.a: By default they don't run, unless you use --force-handlers or force_handlers: true.

roles-organizing-your-code.core: A role packages tasks, handlers, templates, files, defaults and metadata in a standard directory layout, so it can be reused and shared (Ansible Galaxy, collections). Playbooks then just assign roles to host groups. Good roles do one thing (nginx, postgres, hardening), expose defaults as their interface, and are tested with Molecule.

first_principles.problem: A 2,000-line playbook mixes nginx, users and monitoring, and nobody can reuse any part.

analogy.title: Kitchen stations in a restaurant
analogy.story: The grill, pastry and salad stations each have their own tools and recipes; the head chef assigns stations to orders.
analogy.breaks: Stations share a pass; roles should avoid hidden shared state.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Readable playbook; each role reusable elsewhere.

code.text:
# site.yml
- hosts: role_web
  become: true
  roles:
    - common_hardening
    - { role: nginx, nginx_port: 8080 }
    - node_exporter

check.a: Testing roles by spinning up containers/VMs, applying the role, verifying results and checking idempotency.

tags-selective-execution.core: Tags label tasks, blocks or roles so you can run or skip subsets with --tags or --skip-tags: just deploy the config, or skip slow package installs. Special tags `always` and `never` control default inclusion. Tags speed up targeted runs but can hide dependencies; a tagged run may skip a task that later tasks rely on.

first_principles.problem: Updating one config file requires a 20-minute full playbook run.
truths: Not every run needs every task.

analogy.title: Chapter bookmarks
analogy.story: Jump straight to the chapter you need, but you might miss context from earlier pages.
analogy.breaks: Readers can flip back; skipped tasks just don't run.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 30-second targeted run; wipe only with --tags wipe_cache.

code.text:
- name: Deploy app config
  ansible.builtin.template: { src: app.yml.j2, dest: /etc/app.yml }
  tags: [config]
- name: Wipe cache (opt-in)
  ansible.builtin.file: { path: /var/cache/app, state: absent }
  tags: [never, wipe_cache]
# ansible-playbook site.yml --tags config

check.a: The task is skipped unless one of its other tags is explicitly requested with --tags.

ansible-vault-keeping-secrets-safe.core: Ansible Vault encrypts files or single variables with AES-256 so secrets can live in Git safely. Playbooks decrypt them at runtime with a vault password, supplied via a prompt, a file or a script that fetches it from a secrets manager. Use vault IDs for different environments, and consider lookups to HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for rotation and auditing.

first_principles.problem: Database passwords sit in plaintext group_vars in the Git repository.
truths: Secrets must not be readable in Git.
Passwords for decryption need protecting too.
derivation: Supply password via **script** from a secrets manager.

analogy.title: A locked box in a shared cupboard
analogy.story: Everyone can see the box, but only those with the key can read what's inside.
analogy.breaks: Boxes can't be copied; encrypted files can be brute-forced if the password is weak.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Secret in Git is ciphertext; decrypted only at runtime.

code.text:
ansible-vault encrypt_string --vault-id prod@scripts/vault-pass.sh 'S3cr3t!' --name db_password
# db_password: !vault |
#   $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;prod
#   6231...
ansible-playbook site.yml --vault-id prod@scripts/vault-pass.sh

check.q: Why add no_log: true to tasks using secrets?
check.a: To stop the decrypted values appearing in task output and logs.
